title: 11. Answer Keys, Diagnostic Index & Exam Routine
blocks: A consolidation reference rather than new drills: how to review a wrong answer, a diagnostic index of the highest-frequency errors with the single rule that fixes each, the full chapter map, and the ten-minute exam self-edit routine.

Every exercise in this course is self-checking: when you submit an answer, the platform shows you the correct version, the reason it is correct, and a Bengali note explaining the underlying rule. This final chapter is not another set of drills. It is a consolidation reference, the place to come back to when a mistake recurs, so you can find the one rule that fixes a whole family of errors. Use it as a diagnostic index: identify the error you keep making, then re-read the rule and the chapter it comes from.
11.1 How to review an incorrect answer
When you get an item wrong, do not simply read the correct answer and move on. Spend thirty seconds diagnosing it, because the same error type will return in your own writing.
Read the model answer and the reason together, so you see the rule in action, not just the fix.
Name the error type: is it agreement, tense, article, preposition, structure, or a range issue?
Go back to the source chapter for that type (the map is in 11.3) and re-read the one rule that governs it.
Write two fresh sentences of your own that apply the rule correctly. Producing the form, not just recognising it, is what moves it into your active grammar.
11.2 The highest-frequency errors, and the single rule that fixes each
These are the mistakes that appear most often in Bangladeshi scripts. If you internalise this short table, you remove the majority of your recurring errors.
The verb agrees with the true subject, not the nearest noun.
Uncountable nouns take no a/an and no plural.
A finished year takes the past simple, not the present perfect.
‘Since/for’ take a perfect tense, not the present continuous.
Direct-translation prepositions: discuss X; in my opinion.
A dependent clause cannot stand alone (fragment).
Two clauses need more than a comma (comma splice).
Hedge sweeping claims: may, tend to, generally.
After a fronted negative, use question word order.

On exam day, the grammar you have built pays off only if you leave time to apply the self-edit. Reserve the last few minutes of each writing task for a targeted review, running the passes from Chapter 10 in order.

Task 1 (leave ~3 minutes): check every tense against the time frame of the data; check the data prepositions (by, from, to, of); check that “the number of” and “the proportion of” take singular verbs.

Task 2 (leave ~5 minutes): run agreement, article, and preposition passes; confirm no “will” sits in an if-clause; confirm you have a variety of complex sentences and at least one clean high-band structure.
Speaking (in real time): if you hear an agreement or tense slip, self-correct smoothly and move on; a clean self-correction is a sign of control, not weakness.

Knowing a rule and applying it under pressure are different skills, and the gap between them is closed only by the review habit this chapter describes. Candidates who diagnose their recurring errors, return to the governing rule, and then produce fresh correct examples improve far faster than those who only complete drills once. Treat every wrong answer in this course as information about which single rule to revisit. That loop, error to rule to fresh production, is what turns study into a higher band.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Review loop: Wrong answer → name the error type → re-read the rule → write two correct sentences of your own.
Exam routine: Always reserve the final minutes to run the six editing passes in order.

This completes the course. Return to any chapter's exercises to practise until the correct forms feel automatic; the platform will keep scoring you and showing the reason and Bengali note for every item.
